Insilico Medicine - generative-AI drug design, rentosertib in phase 2

how: AI accelerates drug discovery at every step: predicting protein structures from amino-acid sequences (AlphaFold), generating novel molecules optimized for a target (generative chemistry), screening billions of virtual compounds against disease proteins, predicting toxicity and ADMET properties before synthesis, and designing clinical trials with better patient selection. The AI proposes; chemists synthesize and test the most promising candidates; the results feed back into the models. The loop - predict, make, test, learn - runs far faster than traditional screening.
name: AI-Discovered Medicines
principles: Structure is destiny: knowing a protein's shape unlocks designing molecules to fit it.
Generation beats screening: designing molecules beats testing random ones.
Data is the fuel: every tested molecule improves the next prediction.
The loop is the product: predict-make-test-learn cycles compound.
AI proposes, humans dispose: models suggest; experiments and regulators decide.

public.i: Drug discovery began as observation: humans learned which plants healed by trial and error over millennia.
public.k: For most of history, medicines came from nature - willow bark for pain, foxglove for the heart, cinchona bark for malaria - discovered by observation and refined by tradition. The method was slow but effective: thousands of years of human trials. Every modern drug traces its lineage to this observational beginning.
public.title: Herbal Medicine: The First Drug Discovery

public.i: Isolation turned folk remedies into chemistry: the active molecule, purified and dosed.
public.k: In 1804 Friedrich Sertuerner isolated morphine from opium, and by mid-century chemists were purifying active compounds - quinine, atropine - and synthesizing them, culminating in aspirin's synthesis in 1853 and Bayer's commercialization in 1899. The isolation era proved drugs were molecules, not mixtures. Chemistry could now improve on nature.
public.title: Isolation Era: From Bark to Molecule

public.i: Salvarsan proved drugs could be designed, not just found - the birth of medicinal chemistry.
public.k: Paul Ehrlich's team developed Salvarsan in 1909 - compound 606 - the first drug designed through systematic chemical modification to kill a pathogen (syphilis) while sparing the patient. It was toxic by modern standards but proved the principle: molecules could be engineered as medicines. Drug discovery became a design discipline.
public.title: Salvarsan: The First Designed Drug

public.i: Penicillin proved nature was still the best chemist - and screening was the way to ask.
public.k: Fleming's 1928 observation of penicillin's antibacterial action, developed into a drug by Florey and Chain in the 1940s, launched the antibiotic era. The lesson: screen natural products systematically and nature provides. Pharmaceutical companies built vast natural-product screening programs - the industrialization of serendipity.
public.srcn: Fleming 1929; Florey and Chain development histories.
public.title: Penicillin: Screening Nature

public.i: The golden age of screening found most of our antibiotics - and exhausted the easy wins.
public.k: Selman Waksman's systematic screening of soil microbes (streptomycin, 1943) launched the golden age: through the 1940s-70s, screening programs discovered most major antibiotic classes. But by the 1970s the easy discoveries were made - screens kept rediscovering known compounds. The field needed rational design, not just luck.
public.srcn: Waksman screening histories; antibiotic discovery literature.
public.title: The Golden Age of Screening

public.i: Captopril proved structure-based design works: see the target, design the drug.
public.k: Captopril, approved in 1975, was among the first drugs designed from knowledge of its target's structure - blocking the ACE enzyme to lower blood pressure. The structure-based approach - determine the protein's shape, design a molecule to fit - became the rational alternative to blind screening. Seeing the target changed everything.
public.srcn: Captopril development histories; ACE inhibitor literature.
public.title: Captopril: Design from Structure

public.i: Combinatorial chemistry and high-throughput screening industrialized molecule testing - millions of compounds, robotic speed.
public.k: Through the 1980s-90s, combinatorial chemistry generated vast compound libraries and high-throughput screening tested them robotically against targets. The industry could now test millions of molecules. But the hit rates disappointed: random diversity was not the same as designed quality. The brute-force era taught that smarter beats bigger.
public.srcn: Combinatorial chemistry histories; HTS industry literature.
public.title: Combinatorial Chemistry: Brute Force

public.i: The Human Genome Project promised a target for every disease - the raw material AI would later mine.
public.k: Launched in 1990, the Human Genome Project set out to read all three billion base pairs of human DNA - and with it, every potential drug target. Completed in 2003, it revealed roughly 20,000 genes. The genome was a parts list; the challenge was figuring out what the parts did. That interpretation problem awaited machine learning.
public.title: The Genome Project Begins

public.i: Genomics met drug targets: the druggable genome became the industry's map.
public.k: Through the 2000s, genomics identified disease genes at scale - and the industry mapped the druggable genome: the subset of proteins that drugs could plausibly target. Target validation became the bottleneck: knowing a gene was involved did not mean drugging it would work. The map was drawn; navigating it required better tools.
public.title: Mapping the Druggable Genome

public.i: Deep learning's rise gave drug discovery its future engine - though nobody knew it yet.
public.k: Hinton's 2006 deep-belief networks and the 2012 ImageNet breakthrough proved deep neural networks could learn complex patterns from data. The methods were built for images and speech, but their pattern-learning power applied anywhere data was abundant. Drug discovery - drowning in molecular data - was the perfect next domain.
public.title: Deep Learning Rises

public.i: Early ML models predicted molecular properties - the first AI foothold in drug chemistry.
public.k: In 2012-2014, researchers applied machine learning to QSAR - quantitative structure-activity relationships - predicting a molecule's properties from its structure far faster than experiments. Merck's 2012 QSAR challenge drew ML researchers to drug data. The models were narrow but real: AI could predict chemistry.
public.srcn: Merck QSAR challenge, 2012; early ML-chemistry literature.
public.title: Machine Learning Meets Molecules

public.i: Atomwise proved AI could screen billions of compounds virtually - the first AI drug startup.
public.k: Atomwise, founded in 2012, built deep-learning models for virtual screening - predicting which molecules bind a target without synthesizing them. Its Ebola and multiple-sclerosis screening projects drew attention. The pitch was compelling: screen billions computationally, synthesize only the best. Virtual screening became AI's first drug-discovery product.
public.title: Atomwise: AI Virtual Screening

public.i: Insilico Medicine bet on generative AI: design molecules from scratch, don't just screen them.
public.k: Insilico Medicine, founded in 2014, pioneered generative chemistry - AI models that design novel molecules optimized for a target, rather than screening existing libraries. The generative approach promised to explore chemical space far beyond known compounds. It was a bolder bet than screening: creation, not selection.
public.srcn: Insilico Medicine founding records; generative-chemistry literature.
public.title: Insilico Bets on Generative Chemistry

public.i: AlphaFold won CASP13 - protein folding, biology's 50-year grand challenge, fell to AI.
public.k: DeepMind's AlphaFold won the CASP13 protein-structure prediction competition in 2018 by a wide margin, predicting protein shapes from sequences with unprecedented accuracy. The result stunned structural biologists: a grand challenge that had resisted decades of effort yielded to deep learning. Drug design's key input - protein structures - was about to become abundant.
public.srcn: CASP13 results; Senior et al., Nature, 2020.
public.title: AlphaFold Wins CASP13

public.i: Generative molecule design went mainstream: the papers that launched a hundred startups.
public.k: Through 2018-2019, papers on generative molecular design - variational autoencoders, reinforcement learning for molecules - proliferated, and AI drug startups multiplied: Exscientia, BenevolentAI, Recursion, and dozens more. Venture funding poured in. The field's question shifted from whether AI could help to how fast it could deliver drugs.
public.title: Generative Design Goes Mainstream

public.i: AlphaFold2 solved protein folding - and DeepMind gave the solution to the world.
public.k: AlphaFold2's 2020 CASP14 performance achieved experimental-level accuracy in protein-structure prediction, effectively solving the 50-year folding problem. DeepMind then released predicted structures for nearly every known protein free. Overnight, drug designers had structural starting points for most of the druggable genome - the key input, democratized.
public.srcn: Jumper et al., Nature, 2021; AlphaFold Database release.
public.title: AlphaFold2 Solves Protein Folding

public.i: DSP-1181 entered trials - the first AI-designed drug tested in humans.
public.k: In 2020, DSP-1181 - a long-acting serotonin receptor antagonist designed with Exscientia's AI platform in partnership with Sumitomo Dainippon - entered phase 1 trials: the first drug candidate with AI-designed origins to reach humans. The design had taken months, not years. The milestone was symbolic and substantive: AI-designed molecules were now clinical reality.
public.title: DSP-1181: The First AI-Designed Drug in Trials

public.i: AI drug pipelines multiplied: dozens of candidates, billions in pharma partnerships.
public.k: Through 2021, AI drug companies built real pipelines - Exscientia, Insilico, Recursion, Relay, and others advanced candidates toward and into the clinic, while big pharma signed AI partnerships worth billions in potential milestones. The industry structure shifted: AI platforms became the R&D engine, pharma the development muscle. The pipeline was real; the verdicts were pending.
public.srcn: Company pipeline disclosures; pharma-AI partnership announcements, 2021.
public.title: The AI Pipeline Multiplies

public.i: The AlphaFold Database reached 200 million structures - biology's parts catalog, free to all.
public.k: DeepMind and EMBL-EBI released the AlphaFold Database with over 200 million predicted protein structures in 2021-2022 - essentially every known protein, free for any researcher. Academic labs that could never afford structural biology now had starting structures. The database became one of the most-used resources in life science.
public.srcn: AlphaFold Database release; Varadi et al., 2022.
public.title: 200 Million Structures, Free

public.i: AI-designed drugs reached phase 2 - the efficacy question was now being asked.
public.k: Through 2022, AI-designed candidates advanced to phase 2 efficacy trials: Insilico's rentosertib for fibrosis, Exscientia's oncology candidates, and others. The field moved from safety to the harder question: do AI-designed drugs work? Early readouts were mixed - the honest, expected result for a new paradigm.
public.title: Phase 2: The Efficacy Question

public.i: Honest failures arrived: DSP-1181's trial was discontinued - the field learned in public.
public.k: In 2022, the DSP-1181 phase 1 trial was discontinued for strategic reasons - the first AI-designed drug's clinical journey ended without fanfare. The field absorbed the lesson maturely: most drug candidates fail, AI-designed or not. The failure rate, not the origin story, would judge the paradigm. Honest accounting replaced hype.
public.title: Honest Failures: The Field Grows Up

public.i: Rentosertib's phase 2a data showed AI-designed drugs can produce real efficacy signals.
public.k: Insilico Medicine reported phase 2a results for rentosertib (ISM001-055) in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis in 2023 - a generative-AI-designed TNIK inhibitor showing dose-dependent efficacy signals. It was among the strongest efficacy readouts for an AI-designed drug. The result suggested the paradigm could produce genuinely novel, working medicines.
public.title: Rentosertib: Efficacy Signals

public.i: LLMs entered drug design: the ChatGPT moment reached chemistry.
public.k: In 2023, large language models were applied to drug discovery - molecular LLMs trained on chemical literature, agentic systems planning syntheses, and natural-language interfaces to design tools. The LLM wave brought new talent and new interfaces to the field. Chemistry gained a conversational front end.
public.title: LLMs Enter the Lab

public.i: AlphaFold3 predicted protein-ligand interactions - the drug-design question, directly.
public.k: DeepMind released AlphaFold3 in 2024, predicting how proteins interact with ligands - including drug molecules - plus DNA, RNA, and modifications. The advance addressed drug design's direct question: will this molecule bind that protein? Isomorphic Labs, DeepMind's drug-discovery spinoff, built its pipeline on the technology.
public.srcn: Abramson et al., Nature, 2024; Isomorphic Labs disclosures.
public.title: AlphaFold3: Predicting Drug Binding

public.i: Big pharma's AI deals reached tens of billions - the industry's R&D model was changing.
public.k: Through 2024, pharmaceutical giants signed AI partnerships at unprecedented scale - Sanofi, Bristol Myers Squibb, Eli Lilly, and others committing billions in milestones to AI platforms. The deal structure revealed the new division of labor: AI companies discover, pharma develops. The R&D model had permanently changed.
public.title: Pharma Goes All-In on AI

public.i: AI-designed drugs advanced through phase 2 with growing datasets - the verdicts accumulated.
public.k: Through 2025, multiple AI-designed candidates reported phase 2 results across fibrosis, oncology, and immunology - a growing dataset on whether AI-designed molecules succeed at different rates than traditional ones. The data remained early but suggestive: AI-designed drugs were reaching the clinic faster, with success rates still being measured. The field was building its evidence base.
public.title: The Evidence Base Builds

public.i: Recursion's phenomics platform industrialized biological screening - millions of experiments, AI-read.
public.k: Recursion Pharmaceuticals built one of biology's largest automated laboratories - running millions of cellular experiments weekly, imaged and analyzed by AI. The phenomics platform generated the massive, consistent datasets AI needs. The lesson: AI drug discovery requires industrialized biology, not just clever algorithms.
public.title: Industrialized Biology: Recursion's Platform

public.i: AI entered clinical-trial design: better patient selection, faster trials.
public.k: Through 2025-2026, AI tools for clinical-trial optimization - patient selection via biomarkers, site selection, synthetic control arms - moved into mainstream use, cutting trial costs and timelines. The AI contribution expanded beyond molecule design to the entire development process. Discovery was only the first chapter.
public.srcn: Clinical-trial AI literature and adoption reports, 2025-2026.
public.title: AI Redesigns the Trial
Foundation Models for Biology
public.k: Through 2026, biological foundation models - trained on DNA, protein, and cell-imaging data at massive scale - became the shared substrate of AI drug discovery, with models like ESM, Geneformer, and commercial successors powering target discovery across the industry. The foundation-model pattern from language AI repeated in biology: pretrain broadly, fine-tune specifically. Biology gained its GPT moment.
public.i: Foundation models gave biology the pretrain-then-specialize pattern.
Generative design became standard tooling: every serious drug program now uses it.
public.k: By 2026, generative molecular design and AI screening had become standard tooling in pharmaceutical R&D - used by virtually every major company, whether built internally or licensed. The question was no longer whether to use AI but how well. The technology had crossed from differentiator to infrastructure.
public.title: AI Design Becomes Standard Tooling

public.i: The honest accounting: faster to clinic, success rates still being measured - the evidence status.
public.k: As of 2026, the honest accounting stands: AI-designed drugs reach the clinic markedly faster than traditional timelines, dozens of candidates are in trials, and early efficacy signals are real - but no AI-designed drug has yet been approved, and whether AI improves ultimate success rates remains unproven. The paradigm is productive and unproven at the final hurdle, exactly as the evidence shows.
public.srcn: Synthesis of pipeline and trial data current to 2026.
public.title: The Honest Accounting: Speed Proven, Success Pending

public.i: Regulators adapted: the FDA's frameworks for AI in drug development.
public.k: Through 2026, the FDA developed frameworks for AI/ML in drug development - covering model validation, data integrity, and the use of AI-designed molecules in submissions. Regulatory clarity let companies invest confidently. The rules for algorithmic drug discovery were being written as the drugs advanced.
public.title: Regulating Algorithmic Discovery

public.i: The working version: AI as the industry's R&D engine - fast, standard, and still proving itself.
public.k: By 2026, AI-discovered medicines had reached their working version: AlphaFold structures free to all, generative design standard in every pharma R&D organization, dozens of AI-designed candidates in clinical trials, and the predict-make-test-learn loop running at industrial speed. The technology demonstrably accelerates discovery; whether it improves the odds of approval is the question the next decade of trial readouts will answer.
public.srcn: Synthesis of industry data current to 2026.
public.title: The Working Version: AI-Discovered Medicines Today

public.i: The Signature projection: the loop keeps tightening - design to clinic in months, not years.
public.k: The Signature forward projection for AI drug discovery models the tightening loop: generative design producing clinical candidates in weeks, automated labs testing thousands weekly, AI-optimized trials halving development timelines. The projection expects the first AI-designed drug approval in the late 2020s and success-rate data by the early 2030s. This is Signature projection, clearly labeled: the acceleration is measured, the approval timeline is modeled.
public.title: Signature Projection: The Tightening Loop

status_note: Emerging - dozens of AI-designed candidates in clinical trials; faster discovery timelines demonstrated; no AI-designed drug approved yet as of 2026; success-rate evidence still accumulating.
what: AI-discovered medicines are drugs found or designed with artificial intelligence: predicting protein structures, generating novel molecules, screening billions of virtual compounds, and optimizing clinical trials. It matters because traditional drug discovery takes a decade and billions of dollars per approved drug, with most candidates failing - AI promises to compress timelines, explore vaster chemical space, and improve the odds.
why: The pharmaceutical industry faces declining R&D productivity: costs per approved drug have risen for decades while success rates stagnated. Meanwhile, biological data exploded - genomes, protein structures, screening results - beyond human analysis. AI arrived exactly when the data did, offering to turn the data deluge into designed medicines. Dozens of AI-designed candidates are now in human trials.
